query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single-phase equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy, controlled high-temperature annealing near the service temperature threshold induces a grain-boundary complexion transition from a disordered state to an ordered interfacial film, thereby reducing grain-boundary cohesive strength and leading to embrittlement.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA with disordered grain-boundaries and high toughness.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to a brief annealing treatment at 700–750 °C for 10–30 minutes followed by rapid quenching, designed to trigger a complexion transition at the grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under controlled thermal treatments that mimic near-service temperatures without causing bulk phase transformations, with mechanical testing performed at room and moderately elevated temperatures under service-relevant loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Transformation of the grain-boundary structure from a disordered state to an ordered interfacial film (complexion transition) that is intrinsically more brittle.
generation.mechanism: The brief high-temperature exposure promotes atomic reorganization at the grain boundaries, resulting in the formation of an ordered boundary film. This ordered film reduces the cohesive strength across grain boundaries, thereby lowering the alloy's overall fracture toughness. This mechanism stands in contrast to conventional alloys where embrittlement typically results from grain-boundary segregation or precipitate formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Annealed and rapidly quenched HEA samples will exhibit observable ordered interfacial films at their grain boundaries as detected by high-resolution TEM and grain-boundary spectroscopy. These microstructural changes will correlate with a measurable reduction in fracture toughness relative to as-quenched samples, especially under higher stress conditions.
generation.baseline: The as-quenched HEA state, characterized by a disordered grain-boundary structure and higher toughness.
generation.boundary: The embrittlement effect is expected to be confined to a narrow thermal window (700–750 °C for 10–30 minutes); deviations in annealing temperature or time may not induce the same complexion transition, and prolonged treatments may lead to other effects such as precipitation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of toughness reduction and the sensitivity of the complexion transition to slight variations in thermal treatment parameters and service loading conditions remain to be determined through experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeMnNi HEA samples: the experimental set undergoes the high-temperature annealing (700–750 °C for 10–30 minutes) followed by rapid quenching, and the control set is retained in the as-quenched state. Characterize both sets using high-resolution TEM and grain-boundary spectroscopy (such as EELS or atom probe tomography) to detect the presence or absence of ordered interfacial films. Perform standardized fracture toughness tests on both sets under identical mechanical loading conditions.
measurements: High-resolution TEM images of grain-boundary regions
Grain-boundary chemical state via spectroscopy (EELS or atom probe)
Fracture toughness values from mechanical testing
Correlation of microstructural features with mechanical performance under various stress levels
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if (a) the experimental samples do not exhibit a distinct, ordered interfacial film at the grain boundaries when compared to the control, or (b) there is no significant reduction in fracture toughness in the annealed samples relative to the as-quenched baseline under the same testing conditions.

proposals.intervention: Apply controlled plastic deformation (e.g., cold rolling to varied strain levels) followed by low-temperature annealing
proposals.conditions: Test specimens deformed at room temperature with incremental strains (e.g., 5%, 10%, 20%) and subsequently annealed at ~300–400 °C for defined times to simulate service conditions
proposals.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary compositional heterogeneity induced by deformation‐assisted dynamic segregation
proposals.mechanism: During plastic deformation, enhanced diffusion and solute drag drive certain elements (e.g., Cr, Mn) toward grain boundaries, leading to local composition fluctuations that lower cohesive strength and initiate brittleness. This contrasts with conventional alloys where pre‐existing segregants and precipitates dominate embrittlement.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undeformed, homogeneous baseline, deformed-and-annealed HEA samples would show measurable solute enrichment at grain boundaries (via atom probe tomography) and exhibit reduced toughness in fracture tests, particularly under high strain rate loading. A clear correlation between strain level, extent of segregation, and toughness loss would validate the mechanism.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It proposes a testable mechanism—dynamic segregation induced by mechanical deformation—that could govern brittle behavior in a single-phase HEA and distinguishes it from conventional alloy behavior where grain-boundary segregation is typically inherent.

proposals.intervention: Perform controlled isothermal aging at intermediate temperatures
proposals.conditions: Subject single-phase cast samples to heat treatments at temperatures between 400 °C and 600 °C for various durations (1 to 100 hours) to mimic prolonged high service temperatures
proposals.structural_mediator: Short-range order (SRO) formation near grain boundaries
proposals.mechanism: Although the alloy is initially a single phase, prolonged thermal exposure can induce local atomic ordering, especially near grain boundaries where diffusion is enhanced. The emergent SRO regions may act as embrittled layers, predisposing the alloy to intergranular fracture—distinct from the deleterious intermetallic precipitation seen in conventional alloys.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Aged samples will exhibit diffuse SRO signatures in high-resolution diffraction and local ordering via TEM and electron energy-loss spectroscopy at or near grain boundaries, accompanied by a measurable decline in toughness compared to as-cast samples. The effect should be reversible if aging is below the threshold for SRO formation.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It tests the hypothesis that thermally driven short-range order, and not classical segregation/precipitation, can reduce toughness in HEAs, thereby offering a controlled comparison versus conventional predictions.

proposals.intervention: Introduce cyclic fatigue loading at varying frequencies
proposals.conditions: Examine specimens under controlled cyclic loading (e.g., stress amplitude near yield with frequencies from 0.1 Hz to 10 Hz) at room and moderately elevated temperatures to simulate service fatigue
proposals.structural_mediator: Nanoscale strain-induced precipitation along or near grain boundaries
proposals.mechanism: Under cyclic strain, localized stress fields may overcome the kinetic barriers for nucleation of fine, brittle precipitates even in a compositionally complex matrix. Unlike conventional alloys where precipitate formation is predominantly due to thermal overaging, here mechanical work couples with subtle compositional fluctuations to trigger nano-precipitation that embrittles the grain boundaries.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Fatigue-tested specimens will reveal, via high-resolution TEM and atom-probe tomography, the formation of nanoscale precipitates at high-strain locations (especially along boundaries). Mechanical characterization (e.g., fracture toughness tests) will show a reduced ductility and premature crack propagation compared to static load controls.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It offers a distinct, stress-driven precipitation mechanism for toughness degradation in an initially single-phase HEA, setting up a testable contrast with conventional alloy behavior where grain-boundary precipitation is typically driven by thermal histories.

proposals.intervention: Induce controlled grain-boundary complexion transitions through modest high-temperature annealing
proposals.conditions: Anneal samples near the service temperature threshold (e.g., 700–750 °C) for short durations (e.g., 10–30 minutes) followed by rapid quenching, under conditions designed to trigger complexion transitions at the grain boundaries without bulk phase transformation
proposals.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary complexion (structural state) transition from a disordered to an ordered interfacial film
proposals.mechanism: The hypothesis posits that HEA grain boundaries can undergo a complexion transition under specific thermal conditions. This transition leads to a boundary structure that is intrinsically more brittle even while retaining overall compositional complexity. This mechanism is novel relative to conventional alloys where brittle intermetallic layers form via precipitation rather than an intrinsic change in grain-boundary structure.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Characterization by high-resolution TEM and grain-boundary spectroscopy will reveal a distinct, ordered interfacial film in the annealed specimens, correlating with reduced fracture toughness relative to the as-quenched baseline. The transition should occur only within a narrow thermal window and display sensitivity to service loading conditions (e.g., under high stress, these boundaries would be preferential failure sites).
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It directly tests the emergence of a ductile-to-brittle transition via grain-boundary complexion changes in HEAs, offering a decisive mechanistic difference from conventional alloy embrittlement which relies on segregation and precipitation.

decision.rationale: Direction D is chosen because it directly tests a novel mechanism—that of controlled grain-boundary complexion transitions—in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Its intervention of brief high-temperature annealing followed by rapid quenching is designed to induce an ordered interfacial film at the grain boundaries without triggering bulk phase transformation or conventional precipitation. This approach cleanly contrasts with traditional segregation/precipitation mechanisms observed in conventional alloys and provides a well-defined, controlled comparison between the annealed (transformed) and as-quenched (baseline) states. Although uncertainties remain regarding the sensitivity of the complexion transition to precise thermal conditions and its interaction with service loading, these are accessible with current microscopic and mechanical characterization techniques.
